metaDescription: Three poultry shears fit this budget: SimCoker, Tingling and Jkrycyf. We compare steel grades, stated thickness, locks and grip to show who each one suits.
introParagraphs: Moving up one budget step adds a third model to the poultry-shear field. Alongside the Tingling and the Jkrycyf you now find the SimCoker, a heavy duty shear in 3CR14 stainless steel with an anti-slip handle and a safety lock. Three distinct models is still a small group, so we kept the guide to those three instead of padding it with ordinary scissors or repeat listings.

The tradeoff in this tier is a three-way one. The Tingling is the only listing that publishes a blade thickness, 3.5mm. The SimCoker markets a thicker, more corrosion-resistant steel but does not state a number. The Jkrycyf offers the lowest entry point with an ABS non-slip handle. Choosing among them depends on how much you trust a stated figure compared with a steel grade and a marketing description.

What this cap does not add is a take-apart pivot, serrations or dishwasher approval, which none of the three advertises. Those are features of a higher tier, so all three are hand-wash tools. If you spatchcock a few birds a year and want a dependable spring-assisted shear, this group covers you, and the guide below shows how to separate the three on the details that actually change the cut.

products.name: Tingling Heavy Duty Poultry Shears
products.description:
The Tingling is the only one of the three that publishes a thickness, 3.5mm, in 3Cr stainless steel. That number is the figure often cited for poultry shears that cut through joints, so this is the pick where you can match the spec to the job.

The listing describes a spring-loaded assist and a one-touch safety lock that keeps the blades closed. It also mentions 7cm blades, which concentrate force near the pivot but limit the length of a single slice. The listing does not state a handle material in the excerpt we evaluated, and it does not advertise serrations.

Against the SimCoker, which describes thicker, tougher steel without a number, the Tingling is the evidence-based choice. Against the Jkrycyf, it offers a stated thickness for the same spring-and-lock formula. Check the product page for cleaning guidance, because dishwasher approval is not mentioned in the listing text.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want a published 3.5mm blade to match to spatchcocking.
pros: Short blades give leverage near the pivot

products.name: SimCoker Heavy Duty Poultry Shears
products.description:
The SimCoker listing describes 3CR14 stainless steel that is thicker and more corrosion resistant than ordinary kitchen shears. It is paired with an anti-slip handle, a safety lock and a razor-sharp edge, and the listing says the shears cut meat, vegetables, fruits, noodles, seafood, pizza and barbecue food.

The thickness is described qualitatively, not in millimeters. That makes it harder to compare with the Tingling's published 3.5mm, so treat the claim of a thicker blade as the maker's statement. The broad list of uses suggests an all-purpose heavy duty shear more than a bone specialist.

In use, the anti-slip handle is the useful feature for raw poultry. Compared with the Jkrycyf, the SimCoker offers a different steel grade and a handle described as anti-slip, but no bottle opener function. Compared with the Tingling, it gives up a published thickness. It suits cooks who want an all-around heavy duty pair and are comfortable relying on the maker's steel description.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want an all-around heavy duty shear with an anti-slip handle.

products.name: Jkrycyf Spring Loaded Poultry Shears
products.description:
The Jkrycyf is the cheapest of the three and uses 3Cr13 stainless steel that the listing says retains sharpness and resists rust. It is spring loaded with a safety lock, and the ABS handle is described as comfortable and secure even when wet.

The listing positions it as a multi-purpose heavy duty shear for poultry, meat, herbs and vegetables, and mentions a bottle opener function. No blade thickness is published, so it lacks the evidence the Tingling offers.

It makes sense for someone who cuts chicken a few times a year and wants a locking, spring-assisted tool at the lowest cost. Compared with the SimCoker, it has a spring-loaded claim and the bottle opener function but a different steel grade. Compared with the Tingling, it trades a stated 3.5mm for a lower entry point. The non-slip ABS handle is the part that makes it comfortable for greasy work.
products.bestFor: Occasional cooks who want a spring-loaded shear at the lowest cost.
pros: Spring loaded with a safety lock

buyingCriteria.explanation: Poultry shears are often near 3.5mm because thin blades flex against joints. The Tingling states 3.5mm in 3Cr steel. The SimCoker states 3CR14 steel and a thicker blade without a number. The Jkrycyf states 3Cr13 and no thickness. A steel grade tells you the alloy, not the thickness, so rely on a stated millimeter figure when you can.

A spring reopens the blades so you squeeze once per cut. The Tingling and Jkrycyf explicitly list a spring-loaded design. The SimCoker listing excerpt does not describe a spring in the text we evaluated. Check the product page if a spring matters to you, because a non-spring shear needs you to open the handles by hand.

A lock keeps the blades closed in a drawer. The Tingling lists a one-touch lock, and the SimCoker and Jkrycyf list a safety lock. A one-touch lock is easier to use with one hand. Try the lock a few times before first use, since a stiff lock can be a daily annoyance.

Raw poultry leaves hands greasy, so a non-slip handle matters. The SimCoker lists an anti-slip handle and the Jkrycyf lists non-slip ABS handles. The Tingling does not state a handle material in the excerpt we evaluated. Wipe your hands before cutting no matter which you choose.

Raw poultry residue collects at the pivot, and none of the three advertises a take-apart design or dishwasher approval. Wash by hand with hot soapy water, open the blades fully and dry them before storing. A higher tier adds blades that separate for cleaning. Until then, scrub the pivot area with a brush and keep a separate towel for drying raw-meat tools.

The Tingling uses 3Cr, the SimCoker 3CR14 and the Jkrycyf 3Cr13, all common stainless grades. These can be sharpened with a wet stone, and a soft steel dulls fast. Dry the blades after washing to avoid rust, and do not cut hard bones such as beef ribs. A wet stone is the usual way to restore an edge on these grades.

howWeEvaluated.title: Thickness evidence
howWeEvaluated.description: The Tingling publishes 3.5mm. The SimCoker and Jkrycyf do not, so we scored them on steel grade and description. We did not convert marketing words into numbers.

howWeEvaluated.title: Mechanism
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked each listing for a spring-loaded design and a safety lock. The Tingling and Jkrycyf describe springs, and all three describe a lock.

howWeEvaluated.title: Grip
howWeEvaluated.description: The SimCoker lists an anti-slip handle and the Jkrycyf lists ABS non-slip handles. The Tingling does not state a handle material in our research.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cleaning access
howWeEvaluated.description: None of the three lists take-apart or dishwasher approval. We treated all three as hand-wash tools.

howWeEvaluated.title: Lineup positioning
howWeEvaluated.description: The Tingling leads on published thickness, the SimCoker on a broad heavy duty positioning with an anti-slip handle, and the Jkrycyf on lowest entry cost and the bottle opener function. We used specs and buyer feedback in broad terms and did not claim hands-on testing.

cards.label: Stated number
cards.text: The Tingling's 3.5mm gives you evidence to match against the figure often cited for poultry shears. Pick it when you cut joints.

cards.label: Steel grade
cards.text: The SimCoker and Jkrycyf rely on 3CR14 and 3Cr13 designations. They tell you the alloy but not the thickness. Pick them when cost or grip matters more.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A thicker blade, a spring that reduces hand effort over many cuts and a grip that stays secure when greasy.

faq.q: Which of the three is best for spatchcocking?
faq.a: The Tingling, because it publishes 3.5mm, the thickness often cited for poultry shears. The other two do not state a thickness. If spatchcocking is the main job, that evidence matters.
Only three distinct poultry-shear models fit this budget in our research. We excluded duplicates and ordinary scissors instead of padding the list. A higher tier includes more models.

faq.q: Is the SimCoker thicker than the Tingling?
faq.a: The SimCoker listing says its steel is thicker and tougher than usual but gives no millimeter figure. The Tingling states 3.5mm. We cannot rank them on thickness without a number.
None of the three advertises dishwasher approval in the listing text we evaluated. Check the product page and treat them as hand-wash tools. Open the blades fully and dry them.
A spring reduces hand effort across many cuts, which helps with a whole bird. The Tingling and Jkrycyf list spring-loaded designs. Check the SimCoker page if the spring matters to you.
A higher tier adds blades that separate for cleaning, serrated edges and dishwasher approval. Those help hygiene and grip more than raw cutting power. For occasional use these three are enough.
